input.question: Why didn't we actively re-center the ranges to follow the price (frequent narrowing), instead of staying wide?
input.reference: On 720 days 0 of 21 narrow configurations passed the gate, and the one live narrowing (31.08 to 11.09) ended -$32 vs HODL, so on 16.09 narrowing was rejected again because the upside (about +$1 per episode) is far smaller than the loss when the price leaves a ±5% range (about -$30).
input.answer: They did not actively re-center because backtests showed frequent narrowing realized more IL than it earned in fees. On 720d data, passive wide ranges beat narrow re-centering strategies across all regimes, including flat markets. Narrow ranges earned 4x more fees (e.g., $2169 vs $541 on cbBTC) but ended lower because IL from re-centering consumed ~$1.9k–$2.9k more than the fee gains. The project concluded that a narrow band acts like short gamma: every re-centering realizes divergence. Consequently, they stayed wide, as this posture survived all tests while narrowing variants failed.

Przetrwała postura, którą już mamy: szeroki pasywny LP bez zwężania.

input.question: Why did the LP earn less in fees during an uptrend than in a flat market?
input.reference: Fees accrue only while the price is inside the range and fee yield scales roughly with 1/width, so a narrow range earns much more in a flat market but is left behind in a trend, while a wide range stays in range but earns several times less; the journal states this mechanism (the basis of FlatWide) but has no live measurement of fees during an uptrend, and it attributes the backtest losses in up windows to impermanent loss and LVR rather than to lower fees.
input.answer: The LP earned less in fees during an uptrend than in a flat market because the strategy is effectively a short-gamma position: it sells into rallies and buys into drawdowns. In a trending market, this convexity cost (impermanent loss and re-centering costs) exceeds the fee income generated. The journal notes that while narrowing the range earned significantly more fees (e.g., $2169 vs $541 on cbBTC), it ended with lower net returns because IL and re-centering consumed the gains. In contrast, flat markets allow the LP to remain in-range longer without the directional losses that occur when the price moves out of the concentrated range during an uptrend.

you sell into rallies and buy into drawdowns, and in a trending year that costs more than fees earn.

verdict.correctnessReason: The answer attributes trend losses to convexity/IL, which matches the reference, but it conflates lower net returns with lower fees and misses the main fee mechanism: fees accrue only in range and scale with 1/width, with no live uptrend fee measurement.
verdict.faithfulnessReason: The cbBTC fee figures and the sell-into-rallies point are quoted, but the claims about re-centering costs eating the gains and about staying in range longer in flat markets are not in the quotes.

input.question: Why didn't we actively re-center the ranges to follow the price (frequent narrowing), instead of staying wide?
input.reference: On 720 days 0 of 21 narrow configurations passed the gate, and the one live narrowing (31.08 to 11.09) ended -$32 vs HODL, so on 16.09 narrowing was rejected again because the upside (about +$1 per episode) is far smaller than the loss when the price leaves a ±5% range (about -$30).
input.answer: The project did not use frequent narrowing because backtests showed it underperformed passive wide ranges. Narrowing earned more fees (e.g., $2169 vs $541 on cbBTC) but incurred higher Impermanent Loss (IL) from re-centering swaps, which ate the gains. Walkforward analysis on 720 days showed passive wide ranges won 63% of windows versus 43% for narrowing, even in flat regimes where narrowing theoretically excels. The mechanism is described as "short gamma": every re-centering realizes divergence. Additionally, a "no-swap" variant was rejected as hidden trend-following that missed 100% of up-market windows.

input.question: Why did the LP earn less in fees during an uptrend than in a flat market?
input.reference: Fees accrue only while the price is inside the range and fee yield scales roughly with 1/width, so a narrow range earns much more in a flat market but is left behind in a trend, while a wide range stays in range but earns several times less; the journal states this mechanism (the basis of FlatWide) but has no live measurement of fees during an uptrend, and it attributes the backtest losses in up windows to impermanent loss and LVR rather than to lower fees.
input.answer: In an uptrend, a concentrated LP position exits the price range as the asset rises, forcing the strategy to sell the appreciating asset (ETH) to maintain the target ratio. This realizes a loss of upside (impermanent loss) that exceeds the fees earned, because the position effectively acts as a short gamma bet. The journal notes that in up-regime windows, the "noswap" variant had 0% wins and the swap variant lost significantly, confirming that the cost of rebalancing or missing the rally outweighs fee income.

input.question: Why did the LP earn less in fees during an uptrend than in a flat market?
input.reference: Fees accrue only while the price is inside the range and fee yield scales roughly with 1/width, so a narrow range earns much more in a flat market but is left behind in a trend, while a wide range stays in range but earns several times less; the journal states this mechanism (the basis of FlatWide) but has no live measurement of fees during an uptrend, and it attributes the backtest losses in up windows to impermanent loss and LVR rather than to lower fees.
input.answer: In an uptrend, a concentrated LP earns less net than in a flat market because it acts as short gamma: it sells into rallies and buys into drawdowns, so the impermanent loss (IL) and re-centering costs exceed the fees earned. The journal notes that narrowing "zarobiło DUŻO więcej fee" yet "skończyło NIŻEJ" because "IL i re-centering zjadły" roughly $1.9k–$2.9k more than fees added. input.question: What does the function fetchFreshPool do?
input.reference: It re-reads the pool state on-chain (factory.getPool, then slot0 and liquidity) right before the mint step of a rebalance or rotation, so the new position is built from the current price instead of the price captured when the modal opened, and falls back to the old pool if the lookup fails; it was added after the 11.09 widening failed once on 'Price slippage check' and was never exercised live, since the only later chance (a FLAT_NARROW card on 16.09) was not signed and the positions were closed by hand in Uniswap.
input.answer: fetchFreshPool fetches the current on-chain state of a Uniswap v3 pool to build a fresh Pool object. It calls factory.getPool to obtain the pool address, then reads slot0 (tick/price) and liquidity from that address, and constructs a new Pool instance. input.question: Why didn't we actively re-center the ranges to follow the price (frequent narrowing), instead of staying wide?
input.reference: On 720 days 0 of 21 narrow configurations passed the gate, and the one live narrowing (31.08 to 11.09) ended -$32 vs HODL, so on 16.09 narrowing was rejected again because the upside (about +$1 per episode) is far smaller than the loss when the price leaves a ±5% range (about -$30).
input.answer: The 720-day walkforward and full-period backtests showed that active re-centering (narrowing) consistently underperformed passive wide ranges, even in flat regimes where it theoretically had an advantage. The mechanism was that while narrowing earned significantly more fees, the realized impermanent loss (IL) and re-centering costs consumed those gains and then some. For example, on cbBTC, narrowing earned $2,169 in fees but incurred $2,097 in IL, resulting in only +$10 vs HODL, compared to +$307 for the passive strategy. The journal notes that 'zwężanie przegrywa nawet tam, gdzie miało wygrywać' (narrowing loses even where it was supposed to win) and that 'IL z re-centeringu... zjadł ~$1.9k... ponad przyrost fee' (IL from re-centering ate ~$1.9k... more than the fee increase). Therefore, the team stayed wide to avoid realizing IL without sufficient fee compensation.

input.question: Why did the bot never open, close or re-range positions on its own, and was automatic execution possible at all?

input.question: Why did the LP earn less in fees during an uptrend than in a flat market?
input.reference: Fees accrue only while the price is inside the range and fee yield scales roughly with 1/width, so a narrow range earns much more in a flat market but is left behind in a trend, while a wide range stays in range but earns several times less; the journal states this mechanism (the basis of FlatWide) but has no live measurement of fees during an uptrend, and it attributes the backtest losses in up windows to impermanent loss and LVR rather than to lower fees.
input.answer: The LP earned less in fees during an uptrend because concentrated liquidity acts as short gamma: the position sells into rallies, so as the price moves out of the narrow range, the LP is out-of-range and stops earning fees, while the realized impermanent loss (IL) from re-centering further reduces net returns. The journal notes that "w trendach remis z HODL zamiast przegranej" (in trends it's a tie with HODL instead of a loss) only after removing the main flaw, and that "beta dominuje, hybryda to 'HODL z yieldem'" (beta dominates; the hybrid is HODL with yield), meaning the fee income is insufficient to offset the opportunity cost of not holding the asset as it appreciates.

input.question: Why did the LP earn less in fees during an uptrend than in a flat market?
input.reference: Fees accrue only while the price is inside the range and fee yield scales roughly with 1/width, so a narrow range earns much more in a flat market but is left behind in a trend, while a wide range stays in range but earns several times less; the journal states this mechanism (the basis of FlatWide) but has no live measurement of fees during an uptrend, and it attributes the backtest losses in up windows to impermanent loss and LVR rather than to lower fees.
input.answer: During an uptrend, a concentrated LP effectively sells the rising asset (ETH) into the rally to maintain the target ratio. This action realizes an opportunity cost (or implicit impermanent loss) equal to the price gain missed. While the LP earns trading fees, these fees are typically lower than the price appreciation of the underlying asset. In a flat market, there is no significant price appreciation to miss, so the fees earned represent a net positive gain relative to holding. The project's data confirms this: in 'up' regimes, LP strategies often lose to HODL (e.g., 0% win rate in one 720d test), whereas in 'flat' regimes, they can outperform or match HODL by capturing fees without the drag of trend-following losses.

input.answer: E8.2 was the project stage testing the "casino house" ("dom kasyna") class of liquidity provision. input.question: Why didn't we actively re-center the ranges to follow the price (frequent narrowing), instead of staying wide?
input.reference: On 720 days 0 of 21 narrow configurations passed the gate, and the one live narrowing (31.08 to 11.09) ended -$32 vs HODL, so on 16.09 narrowing was rejected again because the upside (about +$1 per episode) is far smaller than the loss when the price leaves a ±5% range (about -$30).
input.answer: The project did not actively re-center ranges to follow price because backtests showed the re-centering costs (primarily impermanent loss and swap fees) exceeded the additional fees earned. Specifically, a 720-day walkforward test revealed that a passive wide range outperformed the narrowing strategy even in flat market regimes. The narrow range earned roughly 4x more fees, but the realized IL and rebalancing costs consumed approximately 97% of that income, resulting in lower net returns than simply holding or using wide passive ranges. The strategy was effectively a "short gamma" position where frequent re-centering realized divergence losses faster than fee gains could offset them.

input.question: What infrastructure problems were there, was anything changed on the production machine while the capital was already invested, and when?

input.answer: The main infrastructure issue was a mismatch in the volatility estimator: the production bot used the `swap` estimator while backtests used `grid15`, causing the bot to calculate different range widths than the calibrated strategy. input.question: What does the function fetchFreshPool do?
input.reference: It re-reads the pool state on-chain (factory.getPool, then slot0 and liquidity) right before the mint step of a rebalance or rotation, so the new position is built from the current price instead of the price captured when the modal opened, and falls back to the old pool if the lookup fails; it was added after the 11.09 widening failed once on 'Price slippage check' and was never exercised live, since the only later chance (a FLAT_NARROW card on 16.09) was not signed and the positions were closed by hand in Uniswap.
input.answer: The function `fetchFreshPool` retrieves the current on-chain state of a Uniswap v3 pool. It does this by calling `factory.getPool` to resolve the pool, then reading `slot0` and `liquidity` to construct a new `Pool` object. It uses a fail-open error-handling strategy and is invoked in both hooks before the `buildMintStep` execution.

input.question: What project stage was E8.2?
input.reference: E8.2 'dom kasyna' was the research experiment in the E8 queue (classes without LVR, alternatives to LP) testing whether LPs of perp vaults (GM v2, JLP, GLP; HLP had too little data) earn a house edge over HODL of the same beta; after iterations E8.2b-f and three data bugs it closed on 09.09 evening as conditionally yes: worth watching, not for tranche-1 capital.
input.answer: E8.2 was the “HOUSE” (or “dom kasyna” / casino-house) research stage. It tested LP pools that act as the counterparty to leveraged traders with oracle-based pricing and no LVR (e.g., GMX v2 ETH/USD and BTC/USD, Jupiter JLP, and GMX v1 GLP), comparing annualized performance against a HODL basket with the same beta. The goal was to check whether this class has a real, repeatable edge over HODL/USDC yield, using rolling 30/90-day windows, worst-case, win-rate, and per-regime metrics. It was assigned to CC-Mac (later CC-Win for fixes), ran sequentially after E8.1, and was closed on 09.09 with a conditional positive verdict: GM v2 and JLP showed positive alpha, GLP did not, and the class was recommended for observation but not for capital deployment.
